coverage.note: Four items named no street address at all: a jet skidding off a runway near Porterville, a school project on Coast Guard rescue crews, a hit-and-run conviction near Twin Peaks, and the Recology truck rescue that four outlets carried today. Of the five that did, two earned an entry and three did not — see the declined findings.

findings.description: KPMG opened its new San Francisco headquarters here on 1 September 2026, taking 96,300 square feet across three floors of the ten-storey, 307,000-square-foot Foundry Square III, with floor plates of about 35,000 square feet. The firm had held 143,000 square feet at 55 Second Street for two decades and declined to renew that lease; it signed here in 2024 and waited roughly a year for the previous tenant to vacate before fitting out. Anthropic and Intuit also lease space in the building. The floor given over to KPMG's first West Coast Ignition Center, and the interior details the outlet describes, are the firm's fit-out and not facts about the building.

citation.label: Hoodline, “KPMG Shrinks Office by a Third to Join Anthropic on San Francisco's New 'AI Alley',” 2 September 2026

raw.text: KPMG opened its new San Francisco headquarters yesterday at 505 Howard St., shrinking its office footprint by nearly a third even as it moved into the middle of the city's hottest commercial real estate corridor.

resolution.method: EAS exact match on 505 HOWARD ST → parcel 3736183; sf-parcels has blklot 3736183 active, 505–505 HOWARD; the 2025 roll records it as commercial office, built 2014. EAS files the address under parcel 3736001, which sf-parcels reports retired; the active parcel its coordinates fall in is 3736183.

publish.note: The page already existed. Its building block already names Foundry Square III, so the article added nothing to it; the entry carries the news.

findings.description: Nori Mori, a fast-casual Japanese restaurant, is preparing to open in the ground-floor retail of this tower, at the corner of California and Davis streets, with no firm opening date set. It is one of 39 businesses awarded a San Francisco Storefront Opportunity Grant — between $50,000 and $100,000 each, against a three-year lease and public hours — to take on a previously vacant ground-floor storefront. The tower carries about 2,830 square feet of ground-floor retail and already houses Ladle & Leaf, a coffee bodega and, since March 2026, a 12,000-square-foot Citibank branch in space Wells Fargo had held.

citation.label: Hoodline, “Fast-Casual Japanese Spot Nori Mori Lands $100K Grant for FiDi Debut,” 2 September 2026

findings.description: Recorded so the hit is not read again. The city and the nonprofit Five Keys planned to move sixty shelter cabins to a vacant triangular lot here, with a three-year lease at $270,000 a year under a letter of intent; the plan was paused on 28 September 2025 and abandoned two days later, and the cabins went to a Bayview lot as storage instead. The story is a year old, the cabins never arrived, and the headline is about the Bayview lot, which the article does not give an address for.

citation.label: Hoodline, “SF Spent $7M on Tiny Cabins, Now They Sit Empty in a Bayview Lot,” 2 September 2026

raw.text: City officials and nonprofit Five Keys had planned to move the 60 cabins to a vacant triangular lot at 428 11th Street, pairing them with on-site addiction treatment services.

publish.note: The headline is the entry, and this one is about a Bayview lot the article never names an address for. Putting it on 428 11th Street's page would tell a reader that the cabins are sitting there, which is the opposite of what happened — the lease fell through in September 2025 and they never came. The lot's own news is that a shelter plan for it collapsed a year ago, and no headline read today says that.

resolution.method: EAS exact match on 428 11TH ST → parcel 3523012; sf-parcels has blklot 3523012 active, 428–428 11TH; the 2025 roll records it as commercial retail.
resolution.note: No page at this path yet; the parcel is the publisher's to seed.

findings.description: A one-bedroom apartment across from Alta Plaza Park was listed at $5,495 a month, and the story is about how renters reacted to it online.

citation.label: Hoodline, “Pacific Heights One-Bedroom Asks $5,495 a Month, Renters Call Landlords 'Demons',” 2 September 2026

raw.text: A one-bedroom apartment across from Alta Plaza Park in Pacific Heights hit the rental market for $5,495 a month

publish.note: An asking rent is not a fact about a building, and it fails the ten-year test twice over: the listing will be stale in a month, and the story is about the reaction to it rather than about the property. The headline also carries the reaction's own words about landlords, which is not something to hang on a building in perpetuity.
